title: Your first chart
summary: A chart turns a list of numbers into a picture you can read in a second. matplotlib draws it: plt.bar() for bars, plt.plot() for a line, each from two lists, one for across (x) and one for up (y), with one value per point.
objectives: Say why a chart beats a list of numbers.
Draw a bar chart and a line chart from two lists.
Explain how x and y values pair up.
Fix a chart whose lists have different lengths.

slides.h: By the end: a year of rain in one picture
slides.say: Sundarpur is a made-up city, so every number here is practice data. Its rainfall month by month is twelve numbers: hard to read as a list, obvious as bars. You’ll draw it in four lines.
points: `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt` loads the charting library; everyone calls it plt.
`plt.bar(x, y)` draws one bar for each pair of values.
`plt.show()` shows the chart. On Sheetah it appears under the code.
p: Sundarpur is a made-up city, so every number here is practice data. Its rainfall month by month is twelve numbers: hard to read as a list, obvious as bars. You’ll draw it in four lines.
`import matplotlib.pyplot as plt` loads the charting library; everyone calls it plt.
`plt.bar(x, y)` draws one bar for each pair of values.
`plt.show()` shows the chart. On Sheetah it appears under the code.

visual.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
rain = [2, 1, 4, 12, 30, 180, 310, 260, 150, 70, 20, 5]
plt.bar(months, rain)
plt.show()

terms: the Python library most charts are drawn with

slides.say: The first x goes with the first y, the second with the second, and so on. So "Jan" gets 2 mm, "Feb" 1 mm. The order of the lists is the order of the bars.
points: x: what each bar is (here, the month).
y: how big it is (the rain).
Swap two values in one list and the chart lies.

lab.intro: Draw bars and lines from two lists. Sheetah checks the chart itself: what kind it is and every bar or point.

tasks.prompt: plt.bar() gives back the bars it drew. What does this print?
tasks.code:

bars = plt.bar(["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"], [3, 5, 2])
print(len(bars))
tasks.explain: One bar for each pair: three days.
hints: Count the pairs, not the total.
